client: I've been really struggling since starting this new job at the marketing agency about two months ago. Everyone else on my team seems to know exactly what they're doing, and I'm the only one without any real experience in marketing, so I constantly feel like I'm one mistake away from being exposed as completely out of my depth. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the problem feels pretty concrete — I either know the stuff or I don't.
therapist: It makes a lot of sense that you'd feel that way, especially when you're new and surrounded by people who seem confident and experienced — that kind of pressure is genuinely hard to sit with. I'm also noticing something interesting in what you said: you're describing this as a concrete, fixed reality ("I either know it or I don't"), but I wonder if that framing might actually be making the anxiety feel heavier than it needs to. Can you tell me about a specific moment at work where you felt most like you were "out of your depth" — what was happening, and what thoughts were running through your mind in that moment?

client: There was this team meeting last week where my manager asked everyone to weigh in on a campaign strategy, and when it got to me I basically just echoed what the person before me said because I had no idea what I actually thought. Afterwards I couldn't stop replaying it, thinking everyone must have noticed I was just parroting someone else and that it confirmed I don't belong there. I guess I hear what you're saying about the framing, but it's hard to see it as just a frame when that moment felt so real and embarrassing.
therapist: That moment sounds genuinely uncomfortable, and it's completely understandable that it stuck with you — nobody likes feeling caught off guard in front of their team. I want to gently explore one thing though: you're quite certain that everyone noticed and drew the conclusion that you don't belong, but I'm curious what actual evidence you have for that interpretation versus it being a story your anxious mind constructed after the fact. What do you think someone on your team who *wasn't* feeling self-conscious in that moment might have noticed, if anything?

client: Honestly, I guess if I try to think about it from someone else's perspective, they probably just heard a comment that agreed with the previous one and moved on — it's not like anyone said anything to me afterwards or gave me a weird look. But that almost makes it worse in a way, because I can't tell if they genuinely didn't notice or if they're just being polite and the judgment is happening silently. I know that sounds paranoid, but the uncertainty feels harder to sit with than if someone had just called me out directly.
therapist: That insight you just had — shifting perspectives and recognizing that people likely just moved on — is actually a really meaningful step, even if it doesn't feel like relief yet. What you're describing, where uncertainty feels more threatening than a clear negative outcome, is really common in anxiety; your mind is essentially working overtime to resolve a threat that may not even exist, which is exhausting. I'm wondering — if you genuinely *can't* know what others are silently thinking, what would it look like to make a decision about how to treat yourself in that uncertainty?

client: I think I understand what you're getting at — like, choosing to give myself the benefit of the doubt instead of assuming the worst. But it feels almost dishonest to do that, like I'd be lying to myself, because the doubt is still there and just deciding to be kinder to myself doesn't make the uncertainty go away. I'm not sure I know how to actually do that without it feeling forced or hollow.
therapist: You're touching on something really important here — choosing a kinder interpretation isn't about pretending the doubt doesn't exist, it's more about recognizing that your mind has been automatically defaulting to the *worst* interpretation without much evidence, and gently asking whether that default is actually serving you. It's less like lying to yourself and more like refusing to let one unverified story have all the power. What might it feel like to hold both things at once — "I'm uncertain how people saw that moment, *and* I don't have evidence it went as badly as I fear"?

client: When you put it that way, holding both things at once, it does feel slightly less like I'm forcing something fake. But I think the hard part is that in the actual moment, when I'm sitting at my desk or in another meeting, I don't have the mental space to step back and reason through it like this — the anxious thought just hits and it feels completely true before I've even had a chance to question it. So I guess I'm wondering how you're supposed to actually apply this when everything happens so fast.
therapist: What you're describing is one of the most common and frustrating things about anxiety — the thought arrives fast and feels like fact, long before your reasoning mind has a chance to catch up, and that's actually just how our brains are wired rather than a personal failing. One thing that can help is developing a kind of "interrupt phrase" you practice in calm moments like this one, something short like "I notice I'm assuming the worst again," so that over time it becomes a quicker, more automatic response to the anxious thought rather than a lengthy reasoning process. Would you be open to experimenting with something small like that before your next meeting, just to see what it's like to have even a tiny pause between the thought and believing it completely?

client: I'm willing to try it, but I'm a little skeptical that a phrase is going to feel like anything other than a hollow mantra in the middle of a stressful meeting — like, I can already imagine myself thinking it and then immediately going back to the anxious spiral anyway. I guess my worry is that it becomes just another thing I'm doing wrong if it doesn't work the way it's supposed to. Can it actually make a real difference, or is it more like a first small step toward something bigger?
therapist: Your skepticism is actually really healthy here, and I want to be honest with you — it probably *will* feel hollow at first, and you might slide back into the spiral anyway, and that's completely okay because the goal isn't to stop the anxiety instantly but to gradually build a tiny gap between the thought and your reaction to it. It's also worth noticing what just happened in this conversation: you came in feeling like the problem was completely concrete and unchangeable, and you've already shifted your perspective several times in ways that felt at least a little real to you. So I'd gently reframe the experiment — instead of it being something you can do "wrong," what if you just treated it as information-gathering, noticing what happens without judging whether you did it right?

client: That reframe actually helps a little — taking the pressure off doing it "right" makes it feel slightly more approachable, because my biggest fear was just adding another way to fail to the list. I think I can try treating it as an experiment rather than a test, even if part of me is still bracing for it not to work. It's a bit strange to notice that I have shifted a little during this conversation, because I came in pretty convinced nothing would move.
therapist: That moment of self-awareness — noticing that something *did* shift even when you were convinced it wouldn't — is actually really valuable data about you, because it suggests that the stuck, unchangeable feeling isn't quite as fixed as it seems in your worst moments. It's okay that part of you is still bracing for it not to work; you don't have to be fully convinced for the experiment to be worth trying. What do you think it would mean about you if the experiment *did* help, even just a little?

client: I think if it helped even a little, it would mean that maybe I'm not as stuck as I feel — that there's some part of me that can actually learn to handle this job even without having all the experience everyone else seems to have. But honestly, that's a slightly scary thought too, because if I'm capable of more than I think, then I lose the excuse of just being the inexperienced one who can't help feeling this way. I hadn't really thought about how part of me might be holding onto that story as a kind of protection.
therapist: What you just noticed is genuinely profound — that the "inexperienced one" story, while painful, also offers a kind of shelter from the scarier possibility that you have more agency here than you've been allowing yourself to believe. That's not a flaw or something to judge yourself for; it's actually a very human way of managing uncertainty and self-protection. I'm curious — if you didn't have that story to hide behind, what do you think you'd have to face about yourself or your situation that feels so daunting?

client: I think what I'd have to face is the possibility that I might try my best and still not be good enough — that the inexperience isn't the only obstacle, and that even if I learn the skills, there might be something more fundamental about me that just isn't cut out for this. That feels a lot scarier than blaming it on being new, because being new is temporary but feeling fundamentally not enough is something I've carried around for a long time before this job. I didn't expect this conversation to go somewhere that deep, honestly.
therapist: Thank you for trusting this conversation enough to go somewhere that deep, because what you've just named — that fear of being fundamentally not enough — sounds like it's been quietly underneath a lot of things for a long time, and it makes complete sense that a new, challenging job would bring it right to the surface. That core belief is something worth exploring carefully and gently, because it's likely shaping a lot of what you're experiencing at work in ways that go beyond just needing more marketing knowledge. I want to ask with real care — when you think back, where does that feeling of being "fundamentally not enough" feel like it started for you?

client: That's a question I wasn't prepared for, and I notice I want to deflect a little because it feels like opening something I've kept pretty tightly closed. If I'm honest, I think it goes back to being a kid and always feeling like my achievements were never quite enough to land solidly — like there was always a next bar to clear before I could feel okay about myself. I'm not sure I'm ready to dig all the way into that today, but I can feel that it's connected to what's happening at work in a way I haven't let myself see before.
therapist: It takes real courage to even peek at something you've kept that tightly closed, and I want you to know there's no pressure to open it all at once — the fact that you can feel the connection between that old experience and what's happening now is itself a significant and meaningful thing to notice. That pattern you're describing, where there's always another bar to clear before you're allowed to feel okay, sounds like it's been a very lonely way to move through the world. Whenever you do feel ready to explore that more, I'll be here — but for today, how are you feeling right now, having named it even this much?
